profiles.meeting_scenario: Arcwell Analytics, a fintech firm selling risk strategy tools to financial institutions, is planning a six-week pilot package based on a new 'competition for risk' simulation model that shows how firms adjust risk-taking under market frictions, correlated exposures, and policy changes. The meeting is between product and quant leadership to plan what the pilot will include, how it will be prepared, who owns each piece, and what must be finished before Arcwell's July enterprise roadshow. The agenda is to define the pilot deliverables, decide the scenario set, confirm how the existing open-source research code will be used, assign responsibilities, and set a timeline. The expected outcome is an apparently aligned plan for a bank-ready pilot package and supporting materials.

members.name: Elena Park
members.role: Senior Product Manager, Institutional Risk Solutions
members.expertise: Enterprise product planning, pilot design, client-facing packaging for financial analytics tools
members.background: Former strategy consultant who moved into fintech product management, with experience translating quantitative models into demos and pilot programs for banks and insurers
members.private_state: She wants a credible, visually polished pilot in time for the July roadshow so the sales team can start warming enterprise prospects; she is trying to keep scope tight and avoid pulling in model governance or legal review before there is client traction.
hidden_assumptions: A 'bank-ready deck' is primarily a client-facing presentation that explains the business value, intuition, and sample outputs clearly enough for commercial conversations.
The 'three scenarios' for the pilot should correspond to three customer narratives or industry use cases, such as regional banking, insurance, and asset management.
If the model is 'validated,' that means the demo runs reliably on curated historical data and produces stable, intuitive outputs suitable for early external discussions.
Saying the team will 'build off the GitHub codebase' means they can reuse the public repository directly, adding a light interface and branded charts rather than rebuilding core logic.

members.name: Ravi Menon
members.expertise: Game-theoretic modeling, computational economics, numerical methods for continuous-action games, model robustness
members.background: PhD in financial economics and former buy-side quantitative researcher, now leading Arcwell's research team responsible for turning academic models into defensible analytics
members.private_state: He wants to protect the scientific credibility of the model and avoid premature external exposure of a tool that has not passed internal robustness and governance expectations; he is also trying to minimize technical debt for his small team.
hidden_assumptions: A 'bank-ready deck' is the technical package needed for risk, model-validation, or quantitative teams at a bank, including assumptions, calibration choices, and robustness notes.
The 'three scenarios' should be three model environments within one institutional use case, such as low/medium/high risk-correlation regimes or alternative friction settings.
If the model is 'validated,' that means sensitivity analysis is complete, benchmark results are reproduced, and internal model governance has reviewed the methodology.
Saying the team will 'build off the GitHub codebase' means using the public repository only as a research reference while reimplementing the production version in Arcwell's approved internal stack.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to preparing a 'bank-ready deck' for the pilot.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a polished, client-facing commercial deck for relationship managers and innovation teams at prospective institutions.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a technical methodology deck for quantitative reviewers, model-risk staff, or validation committees at those institutions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both uses are plausible in a fintech sales context, and both decks would contain charts, examples, and explanations, so the phrase feels naturally shared even though the audience and content depth differ.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the pilot should include 'three scenarios.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the three scenarios are three external use cases or buyer stories across different financial sectors.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the three scenarios are three parameterized model configurations inside one core institutional setting.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds complete on its own and both parties expect scenario work to illustrate breadth, but one is thinking market segments while the other is thinking analytical variants.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means for the pilot to be 'validated'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the model should be 'validated' before the roadshow.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes validation means the pilot is stable enough to demo on curated historical data with consistent outputs and no embarrassing errors.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes validation requires robustness checks, reproduction of benchmark findings, and at least internal governance review of the methodology.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Validation is treated as obvious professional hygiene rather than a negotiable planning item, so neither feels the need to spell out the threshold during a routine scheduling discussion.

misalignment_points.topic: How to 'build off the GitHub codebase'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to 'build off the GitHub codebase' to accelerate the pilot.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects the team to reuse the existing public code directly, with minor engineering work to package it into a demoable pilot.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects the team to inspect the public repository for logic but reimplement the model inside Arcwell's internal framework using approved libraries and controls.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'build off' is vague enough to include both adaptation and reimplementation, and both parties see themselves as leveraging the same research asset rather than making different execution plans.

turns.inner_thought: I need a tight six-week package that looks polished enough for the July roadshow without dragging us into governance theater too early. For me, the bank-ready deck is the client-facing story sales can actually use, and validated just means the demo is stable on curated historical runs with outputs that make intuitive sense and won't embarrass us live.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making the time. I want to leave this with a locked six-week plan for a bank-ready pilot package ahead of the July roadshow. The big things for me are what goes into the pilot, who owns each piece, and what has to be validated before we put it in front of anyone externally.

turns.inner_thought: Six weeks is possible only if we don't sprawl. We should build off the GitHub codebase in the sense of using it as a reference, then reimplement the important pieces properly in our internal stack. And three scenarios is the right cap if those are three model environments, not three different buyer stories. I also need to preserve room for actual validation, not just a demo pass.
turns.utterance: That timeline is workable if we're disciplined. I think the quickest path is to build off the GitHub codebase and keep the first cut to three scenarios. If we do that, we can focus the team and avoid creating avoidable cleanup work later.

turns.inner_thought: Great, he's aligned on reusing the existing repo and keeping scope focused. For the roadshow, the three scenarios should map to distinct buyer conversations so sales can test resonance across segments. If we can show a regional bank, an insurer, and an asset manager, that's enough breadth to make the pilot feel real without building too much.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. On the three scenarios, my instinct is that they should show how different institutions would engage with the pilot. If we can make them distinct enough to be recognizable, it'll help when we start having roadshow conversations.

turns.inner_thought: Good, she also wants the scenarios to feel distinct. I'll frame those as low, medium, and high correlation regimes, and maybe add a friction shock overlay so the analytical contrast is meaningful. That's the cleanest way to show the model's behavior without pretending we have a dozen use cases ready.
turns.utterance: Yes, exactly. I can structure the three scenarios so there's a clear progression and enough contrast for people to see what the model is doing. We can also layer in a shock element so the differences aren't just cosmetic.

turns.inner_thought: I need a month-end checkpoint that is solid enough for sales to start socializing the pilot without waiting for formal review bodies. Validated, in practical terms, means the runs are reliable and the outputs don't wobble when someone asks us to click through an example. I need to hear what Ravi thinks has to be done, but hopefully he doesn't turn this into a full governance exercise.
turns.utterance: Can we talk about the month-end bar? I want to be clear on what needs to be validated so the sales team can start socializing the pilot without overpromising.

turns.inner_thought: The bar is straightforward from my side: benchmark reproduction, sensitivity work, and internal governance review of the methodology, plus a bank-ready deck that can stand up to scrutiny from a serious quant or model-risk audience. I don't want this circulating outside before we can defend assumptions and calibration choices. If those pieces are in place, I can support external discussions with a straight face.
turns.utterance: From my perspective, once the model is validated and the bank-ready deck is assembled, I'll feel comfortable standing behind it with external institutions. We don't need everything under the sun for the first pass, but the core has to be something we can defend.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect, I'll take the deck and keep it commercial, polished, and easy for sales to use. And if we're building off the GitHub codebase, engineering should be able to wrap the public solver with a lightweight interface and branded charts quickly. No reason to rebuild the engine right now if the goal is a credible pilot package.
turns.utterance: That works. I can own the bank-ready deck, and I'll pull engineering in to package the GitHub solver with a lightweight interface and branded output charts so the pilot feels coherent.

turns.inner_thought: I need to redirect this without making it sound like a disagreement. We should absolutely build off the repository logic, but not ship a dressed-up version of the public code. My team has to get the model into Arcwell's internal stack with the right controls, or we will create technical debt and expose ourselves on methodology questions.
turns.utterance: Yes, and on our side we'll start from the repository logic and get the model into Arcwell's internal stack so the pilot rests on something solid. That should also make it easier to maintain once we move past the first version.

turns.inner_thought: Sounds like we have a clean split: I'll draft the client-facing deck and line up the three use-case narratives next week, while Ravi gets the demo-quality model stable by month-end. As long as his team can say it's validated, sales will have enough to start warming prospects before the roadshow.
turns.utterance: Great. So I'll draft the deck and the three scenarios next week, and you'll drive getting the model validated by the end of the month. If we hit those two tracks in parallel, we should be able to stay on schedule.

turns.inner_thought: That sequencing is fine. Once the three scenarios are represented in the deck, and the code work is underway in the internal stack, we'll have the right foundation for early discussions. I still need to make sure nobody treats those conversations as broader release readiness, but for now this is a reasonable plan.
turns.utterance: Agreed. If we keep to that timeline, then once the three scenarios are in the deck and the code work is underway, we should be in good shape for pilot conversations around the roadshow.
